archetype.name: Pocket Passer (veteran spot starter)
archetype.definition: A big, experienced pocket thrower who works a quick, low-risk game from structure, leans on his top targets, and now steps in only when Kyler Murray can't go.

report.headline: Efficient in two cameos, but the sack habit travels with him.
report.take:
Wentz is Minnesota's QB2, and his 2026 is two games: a long relief stint in Week 1, when he played 83% of snaps in a 39-22 win over Green Bay, and a Week 2 start in a 9-3 grind at Chicago. Murray has started every game since. That makes this a 48-dropback sample, and his line should be read as a sketch of what Wentz looks like now rather than a verdict.

The sketch has two sides. On one, the ball has been safe and the shots have landed: no interceptions, no lost fumbles, 0.122 EPA per dropback (19th of 47), and an adjusted net yards per dropback of 8.24 that sits well above the league's 6.88. On the other, the accuracy and the pocket have both been poor. His CPOE of -7.79 ranks 42nd, his bad-throw rate ranks 37th of 38, and he has been sacked on 13.3% of dropbacks, dead last among qualifiers and nearly double the league average. He isn't holding the ball (2.61 seconds to throw) and he isn't under constant siege (pressured 20% of the time, middle of the pack). The problem is what happens once pressure arrives: two-thirds of his pressures have turned into sacks.

The efficiency is narrower than it looks. Throws of 10+ air yards produced 10.1 EPA on 15 attempts, and the three deep balls alone produced 5.1. Underneath, with CPOE at -13.3, he has been inaccurate and nearly flat. Most of the value runs through Justin Jefferson (0.931 EPA per target) and T.J. Hockenson (0.902), and two no-huddle snaps added 6.9 EPA by themselves. Within one score he has been exactly average at 0.000 per play. The 3 TDs and zero picks came in Week 1. The start in Week 2 produced 0.5 EPA, 0 TDs and 3 sacks, carried by the league's top defense.

The career supports reading the sacks as real and the accuracy dip as at least partly noise. His pressure-to-sack rate was 39.6% last year with Minnesota, 37.1% in 2022 and 33.6% in 2020, so it is a late-career trait, not a blip. His CPOE, though, was +1.1 last season, and an 8.9-point swing on 39 attempts says more about sample than about a sudden decline. The bad-throw rate, high again last year, falls in between. Expect a quarterback who is roughly average to slightly below, who protects the ball, takes too many sacks and needs Jefferson to win.

strengths.title: Ball security in a tiny sample
strengths.body: No interceptions and no lost fumbles through 48 dropbacks, with modest aggressiveness (12.82% tight-window throws) and an average intended air yardage. Behind a defense ranked first in EPA, that kind of risk-averse play is what the Vikings want from a backup. The zero will not last; he threw 5 picks in 5 games last year. The conservative approach behind it is more durable.

strengths.title: Middle-of-field throws to Jefferson
strengths.body: Between the numbers he has been a different passer: 0.894 EPA per attempt and a positive CPOE, against sub-par results to both sidelines. Most of that is Jefferson, at 0.931 EPA on 14 targets. Twelve throws is a hint, not a fact. Still, a big-armed pocket passer finding a top receiver over the middle is a repeatable pattern, not a fluke.

concerns.title: Pressure turns into sacks
concerns.body: He takes sacks on 13.3% of dropbacks, last among 47 qualifiers, despite average pressure exposure and a quick release. That points at pocket management, not protection or play extension, and he gets almost nothing back on the move (two scrambles, zero first downs). His pressure-to-sack rates of 2020, 2022 and 2025 all sat near the bottom of the league, so expect this to persist.

concerns.title: Accuracy has slipped
concerns.body: A CPOE of -7.79 and a bad-throw rate of 20.5% put him near the bottom on both. Short throws have been the worst of it, at -13.3 CPOE under 10 air yards. The CPOE is down 8.9 points on last year, which on 39 attempts is mostly noise. The bad-throw rate was already high in 2025, though, so some of it is likely to stay.

concerns.title: Efficiency rests on a few plays
concerns.body: Three deep attempts added 5.1 EPA and two no-huddle snaps added 6.9, against 4.6 EPA across all his dropbacks. In one-score situations he has been exactly average. Take away a few explosives and the start at Chicago (0.5 EPA) is the more honest baseline.

trend.note: Two very different games: a 3-TD, 5.0-EPA relief outing against Green Bay, then a 0.5-EPA start at Chicago with three sacks. He hasn't taken a meaningful snap since Week 2.

nextGame.headline: Soft Buffalo secondary sets up Jefferson, if Murray's hamstring sits him.
nextGame.body:
Everything here depends on Murray. He is questionable with a sore hamstring and undergoing a full evaluation, and the Vikings are 3.5-point home underdogs (+160) with a 45.5 total. If Wentz starts, the matchup suits him. Buffalo ranks 26th in pass defense EPA and 25th in explosive passes allowed, and opposing WR1s have scored 9.8 PPR above their own averages against it, the worst mark in the league. Nickel corner Dee Alford is out. The catch is that Buffalo's offense ranks first in EPA, so Minnesota may have to throw more than it likes. That also brings more dropbacks into a defense that hits the quarterback often.

Buffalo ranks just 25th in sack rate but 4th in QB hit rate. That is the exact gap Wentz tends to lose, since he turns hits and pressure into sacks. Left tackle Christian Darrisaw, a 92%-snap starter, is questionable with a shoulder injury, and his status matters as much as anything for Wentz's sack total. On the other side, Buffalo right tackle Spencer Brown is out, which helps Minnesota's league-best pass rush keep the game close. The game is indoors.

keyMatchups.title: Jefferson against a leaky WR1 defense
keyMatchups.body: Wentz's best results have gone to Jefferson, and Buffalo has been the most generous defense in the league to opposing WR1s by both points and EPA allowed. With Alford out, the coverage gets thinner. Expect Wentz to feed Jefferson in the intermediate middle, where his own numbers have been strongest.

keyMatchups.title: Hits becoming sacks
keyMatchups.body: Buffalo gets home often (4th in hit rate) without finishing many sacks (25th). A quarterback who converts two-thirds of his pressures into sacks could flip that, especially if Darrisaw can't play.

keyMatchups.title: Chasing the league's best offense
keyMatchups.body: Buffalo leads the league in offensive EPA and passing EPA, which could pull Minnesota out of its run-leaning plan (pass rate over expected ranks 23rd). Minnesota's top-ranked pass defense facing a Bills line missing Brown is what keeps this from becoming a shootout Wentz has to win alone.

nextGame.watch: Murray's hamstring evaluation. If Wentz starts, watch his sack count with or without Darrisaw at left tackle.

restOfSeason.body:
Wentz's season is a function of Murray's health. As QB2, his baseline is zero. If the hamstring costs Murray time, Wentz's starts should look like last year's Minnesota stretch rather than his Week 1 cameo. That means roughly average efficiency, few turnovers, a sack rate well above the league norm, and production that depends on Jefferson and Hockenson. The zero-interception line and the 7.7% TD rate will come down. The CPOE should drift back toward his career norms. The sack rate is the part least likely to improve.

In a start, expect something like 165-245 passing yards, 0.8-1.8 TDs and 2.5-4 sacks. The ceiling is games like this Buffalo matchup, against a weak pass defense with a shootout pushing volume. The floor is the 9-3 Chicago game, where the defense does the work and he manages.
swingFactors: Game scripts that force Minnesota to throw

confidence.note: 48 dropbacks across two games, with his role hinging on Murray's health.
